title: An-Nisa
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
An-Nisāʾ, "The Women", is the fourth surah of the Qur'an. It is a Madinan surah of 176 verses, and it is above all a surah about the rights and duties that people owe to those in their care. It deals with the orphan and the orphan's property, with marriage and the dowry, with the shares of inheritance, with the treatment of wives and with the limits that protect family life. It then widens to the life of the whole community: justice and trust, obedience to the Messenger ﷺ, the hypocrites, fighting and emigration, prayer in times of danger, and the story of the Children of Israel.

It begins in an unusual way for a surah so full of law. Before it gives any ruling, it speaks to all of humanity and tells them to be mindful of their Lord, who made them from one soul. The rights people owe one another are rights they owe in the sight of Allah, who is always watching. Everything that follows stands on that foundation.

### Where and when it was revealed

Ibn ʿAbbās said that An-Nisāʾ was revealed in Madīnah, in the report of al-ʿAwfī. Ibn Marduwyah recorded similar statements from ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr and from Zayd ibn Thābit. It is therefore counted as a Madinan surah, and the numbering used in this reader gives it 176 verses.

### What the name means

An-Nisāʾ means "The Women". The name stands over a surah that opens with orphans, marriage, the dowry and inheritance. It returns to women's rights again and again: protection from financial abuse inside marriage (verses 19 to 21), the relations that may not be married (22 to 24), and disputes between spouses and justice between wives (128 to 130).

### What the Companions said about it

ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said that there are five verses in An-Nisāʾ that he would prefer to the life of this world and everything in it. Al-Ḥākim recorded this in his Mustadrak. The verses are identified by their opening words:

1. "Indeed, Allah never wrongs ˹anyone˺—even by an atom’s weight" (4:40).
2. "If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you" (4:31).
3. "Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills" (4:48).
4. "If only those ˹hypocrites˺ came to you ˹O Prophet˺—after wronging themselves—seeking Allah’s forgiveness" (4:64).
5. "Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110).

Al-Ḥākim also recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Ask me about Sūrat An-Nisāʾ, for I learned the Qur'an when I was still young." Al-Ḥākim said this hadith is ṣaḥīḥ by the standard of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, although the two of them did not collect it.

### How it connects to Āl ʿImrān

The last verse of Āl ʿImrān ended with an exhortation to taqwa, being mindful of Allah. An-Nisāʾ opens with taqwa too, and this time it comes as a command. The previous surah spoke of battles, of how to treat those who stood against the believers, and of misappropriating the spoils of war, and it took up several other matters besides. An-Nisāʾ turns, in its opening part, to the rights that people owe their own relatives, orphans and wives. These are called ḥuqūq al-ʿibād, the rights of the servants of Allah.

### Why it begins with mindfulness of Allah

Some of these rights can be enforced in court. Ordinary dealings such as buying and selling are like that, and so are leases, tenancies and wages. They can be settled by agreement or arbitration, and if one party falls short, what is owed can be legally recovered.

The rights owed to those in one's charge are different. They include the rights of children, parents, husband and wife, orphans and other relatives. Their fulfilment depends on good conduct, respect, affection, and above all on a heartfelt wish to do what is good for the other person. Such things cannot be weighed on a scale. To settle them fully and exactly by agreement is also far too hard. The only way to fulfil them is to fear Allah and to fear what the life to come will bring. This is taqwa, and its power is greater than the combined power of government and law. That is why the surah opens with the command to taqwa.

### What the surah covers

The opening verses lay the foundation of human society: its single divine origin, the ties of family and mindfulness of Allah (verse 1). The surah then protects the rights and wealth of orphans (2), sets out the rules of marriage with justice and the dowry, including marrying more than one wife (3 and 4), and teaches responsible management of the property of dependents (5 and 6). The law of inheritance, with its fair distribution of wealth, follows at greater length (7 to 14).

Next come the laws on illegal sexual relations and the path of repentance (15 to 18). Then the surah speaks of women's rights in marriage and protection from financial abuse (19 to 21), the marriages that are forbidden in order to preserve family honour and social order (22 to 24), and marriage to bondwomen for those who cannot afford to marry free women (25). A short passage on Allah's grace, guidance and mercy to humanity follows (26 to 28).

From there the surah forbids exploitation, injustice, and harming oneself or others (29 and 30). It names avoiding major sins as the path to forgiveness (31), teaches contentment, divine provision and the rights of heirs (32 and 33), and describes the roles of husbands and wives in the family (34 and 35). It then calls for worship in its fullest sense, from the oneness of Allah to duties toward other people (36 to 38), speaks of Allah's perfect fairness and generosity (39 and 40), and of the Day of Judgment, with its witnesses and its accounting (41 and 42). Purification for prayer, in body and in heart, comes next (43).

A long passage then warns against those who distort scripture and oppose the truth (44 to 47). It declares shirk, associating partners with Allah, to be the one sin that Allah does not forgive (48), and it condemns self-righteousness, false claims and envy (49 to 55). It sets out the final destinations, punishment and reward (56 and 57), and commands justice, trust and obedience to those in authority (58 and 59). It exposes the hypocrisy of those who reject divine judgment (60 to 63), defines true faith as complete submission to the Prophet's ﷺ judgment (64 to 68), and promises those who obey a place among the righteous (69 and 70).

The surah then takes up fighting. It calls for military preparation and exposes those who hang back (71 to 73). It speaks of fighting for Allah's cause and freeing the oppressed (74 and 75), of the battle between faith and the forces of Satan (76), and of those who are afraid to fight and cling to worldly life (77). It teaches that death cannot be escaped and that every event comes from Allah (78 and 79), calls for obedience to the Messenger ﷺ and exposes the double standards of the hypocrites (80 and 81). It calls on people to reflect on the divine origin of the Qur'an (82), to verify news before spreading it (83), and it repeats the call to fight, with each person responsible for himself (84). It speaks of intercession, in good and in evil (85), of returning greetings (86) and of the certainty of the Resurrection (87). It addresses the division over the hypocrites and the matter of divine misguidance (88 to 91), and it gives the law on killing a believer (92 and 93). The surah warns against carelessness in identifying the enemy (94), praises striving in Allah's cause (95 and 96), and describes the fate of those who would not emigrate away from oppression (97 to 99) and the blessings of those who did (100). It ends this section with the concessions for prayer in travel and in danger (101 to 103) and with perseverance in pursuing the enemy (104).

The next passage concerns justice and repentance. It calls for just judgment and warns against pleading for the deceitful (105 to 109). It opens the door of repentance and states that each person answers for his own sin (110 to 112). It records Allah's protection of the Prophet ﷺ from deception (113), the value of good speech and private counsel (114), and the severe consequence of opposing the Messenger ﷺ (115). It returns to shirk and the deceptions of Satan (116 to 121), promises the believers Allah's true reward (122), and teaches that salvation comes through deeds and not wishful thinking (123 and 124). The way of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), true submission to Allah, is held up as the model (125 and 126).

Family law comes back with the rights of women and orphans in marriage (127) and with marital disputes, reconciliation and justice between wives (128 to 130). Allah's sovereignty and the command to be mindful of Him follow (131 to 134), then the command to stand firm for justice (135) and the pillars of true faith (136).

The last long stretch deals again with the hypocrites and then with the Children of Israel. It describes the fate of those who waver in faith (137 to 139), warns against sitting where Allah's signs are mocked (140), and portrays the opportunism and defining traits of the hypocrites (141 to 143). It forbids taking disbelievers as allies (144), states the destination of the hypocrites and the path to salvation (145 to 147), and gives the ethics of speech, including when speaking ill of someone is permitted (148 and 149). It requires belief in all the prophets (150 to 152). It then recounts the demands and transgressions of the Children of Israel (153 and 154), their sins and the truth about ʿĪsā (Jesus) (155 to 159), their punishments and the reward of the righteous among them (160 to 162). It places Muhammad ﷺ within the line of messengers (163 to 165), records Allah's own testimony to his prophethood (166), and speaks of the fate of those who reject and obstruct the truth (167 to 169). A universal call to believe in the Messenger ﷺ follows (170), then a warning against religious extremism and the truth about ʿĪsā (171 and 172). The reward of the humble and the punishment of the arrogant are set side by side (173), and the surah speaks of conclusive proof and the light of guidance (174 and 175). It ends where it began, with inheritance: verse 176 gives the ruling on full siblings, the case known as kalālah.

### In short

- An-Nisāʾ is a Madinan surah of 176 verses. Ibn ʿAbbās said it was revealed in Madīnah, and Ibn Marduwyah recorded the same from ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr and Zayd ibn Thābit.
- It opens, like the end of Āl ʿImrān, with taqwa, because the rights owed to orphans, relatives and wives depend on conscience and the fear of Allah more than on any court.
- Ibn Masʿūd said that five of its verses (4:31, 4:40, 4:48, 4:64 and 4:110) were dearer to him than the life of this world, and Ibn ʿAbbās invited people to ask him about it because he had learned the Qur'an young.
- It moves from orphans, marriage and inheritance, through the community's justice, worship and fighting, to hypocrites, the People of the Book and ʿĪsā, and it closes with the inheritance ruling on kalālah.

1.text:
The surah opens with a call to every human being: "O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women." The call then turns to what people owe to Allah and to one another: "And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties. Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you."

This one verse is the doorway to the whole surah. It does two things at once. It warns people against seizing for themselves what belongs to Allah alone, and it reminds them that they are all children of one father and one mother. That second fact gives life together a warm footing of love, sympathy and concern, so that the rights of relatives, orphans and married couples are met from the heart and not only on paper. The verse that follows turns straight to orphans and the protection of their property.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity!"** Ibn ʿAbbās explained that this wording is general, although it can also be meant for one particular group. One explanation takes it as a call to the people of Makkah, who were the first to hear it. The wider reading is that it takes in every human being, men and women alike, whether alive when the Qur'an came down or born at any time until the Day of Judgment. It is addressed to the human race, not only to the believers.

**"Be mindful of your Lord"** translates ittaqū rabbakum, a command built on taqwā (being mindful of Allah), the word that runs through this verse and through the whole surah. It is often rendered "fear", and it means to fear acting against your Lord. Allah commands His creatures to be mindful of Him by worshipping Him alone, with no partner. Some scholars put it in a few words: obey your Lord. Others said it means to be mindful of His punishment by being obedient to Him. This may be why the Prophet ﷺ used to recite this verse in the address he gave at a wedding. Reciting it in the khuṭbah (sermon) of the nikāḥ (marriage) therefore keeps his Sunnah, his way, alive.

The verse could have used any of Allah's most beautiful names. It chose Rabb, Lord, the One who takes full responsibility for nurturing human beings. People see the marks of that lordship at every moment of their lives. A Being who looks after them so completely deserves all the awe they are able to feel. So the command carries its own wisdom and reason, and the very thought that anyone could rise against such a Lord in defiance is terribly dangerous.

**"Who created you from a single soul"** reminds people of Allah's ability: He made all of them from one person, Ādam (Adam). He could have brought them into being in more than one way. He chose one particular way, a single man as the origin of everyone, and by doing so tied all people together in a strong bond of brotherhood. Ibn ʿAbbās added that people were created through the union of a man and a woman, and that the "single soul" is Ādam's alone, since Ḥawwāʾ's soul was included in his.

**"and from it He created its mate"**. The mate is Ḥawwāʾ (Eve), Ādam's wife. She was created from his left rib, taken from his back while he slept. When Ādam woke and saw her, he was pleased with her and grew fond of her, and the feeling was mutual. An authentic hadith says:

> "Woman was created from a rib. The most curved part of a rib is its upper part. If you try to straighten it, you will break it, and if you leave it alone, it will stay crooked."

A short explanation calls her the mother of all people, as Ādam is their father.

**"and through both He spread countless men and women"**. From Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, Allah created many men and women and scattered them across the world. He made them different in shape, character, colour and language. In the end they will all be gathered, and their return will be to Allah. Other explanations use the words "separated", "spread" and "all over the earth", and speak of scores of human beings, male and female.

**"And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—"**. The command is repeated, this time with the name Allah, and the next words say how people use that name. The Arabic is tasāʾalūna bihi. Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan said it refers to the habit of saying to someone, "I ask you by Allah," and then, "and by the tie of the womb between us." Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it means: be mindful of Allah, the One you call on when you make deals and contracts. Another explanation says people claim their goods and their rights from one another by appealing to Allah's right. To be mindful of Allah here means to protect yourself from Him by obeying Him.

On grammar, the verb is written tassāʾalūna. It stands for tatasāʾalūna, with one tā' merged into the sīn. A variant reading is tasāʾalūna, in which the sīn is not doubled. People also need to hear the point behind the wording. They demand their rights from others in Allah's name and press for what they want. Whoever expects others to fear Allah must therefore fear Him himself.

**"and ˹honour˺ family ties"** translates wal-arḥām, literally "and the wombs". Arḥām is the plural of raḥm, the womb. A mother's womb is the child's home until birth, and it is where blood relationship begins. Keeping up the relationship that comes through it is called ṣilat ar-raḥm, which literally means an umbilical link or bond. Being careless and indifferent toward one's blood relations is qaṭʿ ar-raḥm, cutting that bond, which means cutting off one's kin.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ar-Rabīʿ and others said that the command is to revere the womb by not cutting its ties, but to keep them and honour them. Shorter explanations say the same: be mindful of breaking relations with your blood relatives, or keep the ties of kinship and do not sever them. There is also a second sense, that people claim their rights from one another by the right of kinship and descent.

Another reading puts a different vowel on the last word and joins it to the pronoun in "by Him". The sense is then: be mindful of Allah, in whose name you appeal to one another, and in the name of the wombs. This fits the habit of the time, since people used to implore one another by ties of kinship. The last word of the verse is a warning in any case. It says that any failure to look after close relatives, on the father's side or the mother's, must be avoided.

**"Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you"**. The Arabic word is raqīb, one who watches. Allah watches everything you do and sees how you stand in every circumstance. Another verse says: "For Allah is a Witness over all things" (58:6). An authentic hadith says:

> "Worship Allah as if you see Him, for even though you cannot see Him, He sees you."

This part of the verse encourages a firm certainty that Allah is watching, completely and perfectly. Other explanations call Him a Protector who will question you about what He commanded, in the way of obedience and keeping the ties of kinship. Others say He is heedful of your deeds and will repay you for them, and that nothing you do escapes Him. The words "is ever" show that this is an attribute He always has.

### One father, one mother, and no high or low

All human beings are one by birth. Every person traces back to the same man and the same woman, as father and mother. So people should feel close to one another and deal with each other fairly and kindly, as one large family would. Because of this shared origin, there must be no one high and no one low in race or caste, in colour or language. None of these differences may be made the measure of good or bad, of noble or mean.

Allah also gave a reason for making mankind from a single father and a single mother. It was so that they would feel compassion for one another and be kind to the weaker among them.

This unity of descent grows tighter inside the family. For that reason decent behaviour among relatives matters even more. The verse is therefore not only about faith in the abstract. It asks a person to carry out the rights of humanity, which are mutual sympathy, well-being and the good of everyone, and it asks this on top of the fear of Allah and the fear of the Hereafter.

### Dealings with people are dealings with Allah

Good behaviour toward others is not only a moral point. It is also a matter of personal concern, because everyone is governed by the Almighty and Reckoner, who will decide the eternal future of every human being in the Hereafter and will repay people for what they did in this world. A person should not treat his dealings with others as business between one human being and another. They are business between him and Allah. He should fear Allah's grip and keep inside the limits Allah has set, so as to be saved from His anger.

A hadith reports that Allah said:

> "I will join Myself to the one who strengthens the ties of kinship, and I will separate Myself from the one who severs them."

This shows that a person's attachment to Allah is tested by his relations with other people. Whoever is in fear of Allah when he deals with the rights of others truly reveres Him, and whoever loves other human beings truly loves his Creator. Fair dealing and compassion are basic requirements of any human society. They matter so much to family relations that they rank next to the duty owed to Allah Himself.

### How the Prophet ﷺ used this verse

Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ that Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Bajalī said a delegation from Muḍar came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He saw how they were dressed, in striped woollen clothes, a sign of their poverty. After the Zuhr prayer the Prophet ﷺ stood and gave a speech, in which he recited this verse to its end. He also recited: "O believers! Be mindful of Allah and let every soul look to what ˹deeds˺ it has sent forth for tomorrow" (59:18). Then he urged them to give charity. He spoke of a man who gave ṣadaqah (charity) from his dīnār, from his dirham, from his ṣāʿ (a measure) of wheat and from his ṣāʿ of dates, and so on to the end of the hadith. Aḥmad and the Sunan compilers also collected this narration, from Ibn Masʿūd.

### Keeping the ties of kinship

The hadiths put great weight on the bonds of kinship. The Mishkāt collection records several. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever wants his provision to be made wide and his life to be lengthened should keep good relations with his relatives."

This hadith names two benefits. Fair treatment of one's kin brings a reward in the Hereafter, and it also helps in this life, by easing the narrowness of one's provision and by blessing one's years with more good.

ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madīnah al-Ṭayyibah and he presented himself, the first words he heard from him were:

> "O people, greet one another with salām, feed others, treat your relatives well, and pray at night while people sleep. You will enter Paradise in peace."

Maymūnah, Mother of the Believers, once freed a bondwoman and told the Prophet ﷺ. He said, "Had you given her to your maternal uncle, your reward would have been greater." Islam urges people to free slaves and counts it among the finest of good deeds. Even so, the standing of kinship was rated higher.

He also said:

> "Charity to a needy person is only charity, but charity to a relative is twofold: it is charity and it is kinship."

A simple change in where a gift goes thus earns two kinds of merit.

The opposite attitude is cold-shouldering and severing blood relations. The warnings against it are stern. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "One who breaks the ties of blood will not enter Paradise."

and:

> "Mercy does not descend on a people among whom there is someone who breaks the ties of blood."

### What Allah's watchfulness asks of a person

The closing words move hearts to give people their rights when they fall due. Allah's watchfulness means He knows whatever is in a person's heart: his intentions, his hesitations and his motives. Doing things half-heartedly, as a formality, or from fear of embarrassment, with no real wish to serve, remains unacceptable to Allah. Here too we find why Allah should be feared: because He watches over everyone, always.

This is how the Qur'an usually teaches. It does not set out its laws in sheer cold print, as the governments of this world do. It gives them as education, training and affection, joining the rule to the shaping of minds and hearts.

### The inner reading: mindfulness as a shield

A call comes to the one who stands at the centre of human nature and carries the mark of mortality: take mindfulness as your shelter and cling to it. The life of the servants is in it, and the safe arrival of the travellers.

Mindfulness here means that the servant makes the commands of the Sharīʿah (the revealed law) his shield, so that the arrows of prohibition cannot reach him. There are three levels. At the first, he shelters in the declaration of tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah, and avoids every kind of associating partners with Him. At the second, he shelters in obedience and leaves the path of disobedience behind. At the third, he shelters in caution and runs away from whatever is doubtful. Anyone who climbs these stations truthfully will certainly reach deliverance. The Qur'an says so: "And Allah will deliver those who were mindful ˹of Him˺ to their place of ˹ultimate˺ triumph" (39:61). Elsewhere it says: "And whoever is mindful of Allah, He will make a way out for them and provide for them from sources they could never imagine" (65:2-3). To whoever takes hold of mindfulness, Allah makes easy the road out of every suffering and sends provision from where he had no hope.

### The sister of Bishr Ḥāfī and the spindle

A story shows how far this carefulness can go. The sister of Bishr Ḥāfī went to see Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal. She said, "O Imam of the Muslims! I spin thread on the roof of my house. When the torch of the Ṭāhirids passes by, it may happen that I join threads by the light of that torch. Is this permissible or not?"

Aḥmad asked her first to say who she was. He wanted to know whether she was able to bear such mindfulness. She told him she was the sister of Bishr Ḥāfī. Aḥmad wept. He said this kind of scrupulousness was permissible only in the household of Bishr Ḥāfī, and that it was not fitting for her to do it, so she should be careful not to. Bishr would be happy with her. She should follow her brother's example, in the hope of becoming like him. Then, if she wanted to spin by the glow of the Ṭāhirids' torch, her hand would not obey her. Her brother had reached a degree where his hand refused to obey him whenever it moved toward food that was doubtful in any way.

### When the servant wants only Allah

Allah says that when the servant wants to be negligent of Him, He comes between the servant and his negligence. This is in the report in which Muṣṭafā, the Prophet ﷺ, narrates from his Lord:

> "When I know that what rules my servant's heart is being occupied with Me, I put his appetite into asking Me and conversing with Me. When My servant is like that, he has passion for Me, and I have passion for him. When he is like that and wants to be negligent of Me, I come between him and his negligence. These are My friends in truth. They are the champions. For their sake I remove from the earth those whom they wish to see punished."

On this reading, when a servant wants only Allah, knows only Him and belongs only to Him, Allah turns the face of His own heart toward him. He shuts every door of desire, appetite and want for that servant and clears every other thing out of his heart. Passion for speaking to Allah and listening to Him comes to rule his spirit and heart, and Allah gives him ease on the carpet of passion. He holds the sword of beginningless jealousy over the servant's head. If the servant wished to look at another, crave another or do business with another, Allah would not allow it. Night is turned into day and day into night in the servant's work, and his business with the world's creatures is ruined.

Allah knows how to plunder a servant He wants. Today He entrusts him to the policeman of mindfulness, to keep him under the protection of the Sharīʿah, and mindfulness gives all his movements and his stillness the character of courtesy. Tomorrow He will give him his place in the seat of truthfulness (54:55). That place lies in what the text calls the Presence of At-ness, which means nearness to Him.

On the Day of Resurrection, mindfulness itself will be told to come, because today is the day of its bazaar. Whoever has a portion of it will be settled in a dwelling that matches his portion. Those who knew it well will be seated in the Presence of At-ness, for in the beginningless past Allah decreed: "Indeed, the righteous will be amid Gardens and rivers, at the Seat of Honour in the presence of the Most Powerful Sovereign" (54:54-55).

### The inner reading: pairs, many forms and the Watcher

Allah created everything as a pair, and so every creature was given a spouse. Each was joined to its like and bound to one that resembles it, because being one and being alone belong to Allah alone. They are His attribute, His right and worthy of Him. It has been narrated in one of the books that Allah said, "I have given the things mates so that My unity will be inferred."

The words "spread countless men and women" show His perfect power and the majesty of His lordship. From the offspring of one upright person He brought out many thousands of creatures with different natures and colours, different forms and conduct. Each has its own colour, nature, character, state and aspiration. You will never meet two people who are the same in nature and face, or in form and manner. Glory be to Him, whose decrees never run out and whose knowledge has no limit.

At the end of the verse Allah says that He is watchful over you. A watcher is one who listens to hearts without investigating, who knows deeds without asking, and who has no need to rest in his striving. This is a warning to the servant and eloquent advice for the traveller on the path. It means: you know that I listen to hearts and watch deeds and words, so practise watchfulness and give Me what I am owed.

Watchfulness is that the servant keeps looking at the Real with his heart and keeps the gaze of the Real in front of his eyes. He knows that Allah is not heedless of him, so he is always on guard. Hence Muṣṭafā said, "When you do not like people to see something from you, do not do it while you are alone." In this sense they have sung:

> When you are alone with yourself one day, do not say, "I am alone." Say, "Over me is a Watcher."

### In short

- The verse speaks to all humanity: be mindful of Allah, who made everyone from one soul and made its mate from it, then spread countless men and women from the two of them.
- Being from one father and one mother means no one is high or low by race, caste, colour or language, and it calls for compassion toward the weak and fairness toward everyone.
- People appeal to one another in Allah's name, and they are commanded to honour the ties of the womb. The hadiths promise wide provision and a long life for keeping them, and say that one who breaks them will not enter Paradise.
- Because Allah is always watching, every right must be fulfilled sincerely and from the heart, not as a formality.
- Its inner reading treats mindfulness as a shield with three levels, oneness, obedience and caution, and treats watchfulness as always keeping the gaze of the Real before one's eyes.

2.text:
After the call to honour family ties, the surah turns to the weakest member of the family, the orphan: "Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺, and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables, nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own. For this would indeed be a great sin." The guardian of an orphaned child is usually one of the child's relatives, so this command is one more part of keeping the rights of kinship.

Orphans are the weakest people in a family or in a society. Dealing with them fairly and kindly is therefore the hardest test of whether a person truly fears Allah. They are owed justice and compassion, and their rights must be given the greatest protection possible. The verse names three ways a guardian can wrong them: by holding back their property, by swapping good for bad, and by mixing their wealth with his own.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺"**. "Orphans" translates al-yatāmā, the plural of al-yatīm. In the language, yatīm means the lone or unique one. A pearl that lies alone in its shell is called ad-durr al-yatīm, the orphan pearl. Among animals, a yatīm is a young one whose mother has died. In the terminology of Islamic law, a yatīm is a child whose father has died. When the child reaches puberty he is no longer called a yatīm. A hadith recorded in Mishkāt states it plainly:

> "Orphanhood ends with puberty."

Other explanations agree on what the command means. The orphan's property is to be handed over in full once he reaches adolescence, which is the legal age, and shows sound judgement. The guardian is forbidden to use any part of it or to take it for himself.

**"and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables"** means do not swap bad for good. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and az-Zuhrī said that it means not putting a weak animal of yours in place of a fat animal of the orphan's. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it means not giving something of poor quality for something of good quality. As-Suddī described what guardians used to do. One of them would take a fat sheep from the orphan's flock and put a lean sheep of his own in its place, saying, "A sheep for a sheep." Or he would take a good dirham and give back a fake one, saying, "A dirham for a dirham."

Other explanations put it as taking the unlawful in place of the lawful, which means keeping what is good from the orphan's property and leaving him your own faulty goods. They also say: do not consume the orphan's wealth, which is forbidden to you, while leaving your own wealth, which is lawful for you.

**"nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own"**. The Arabic says: do not devour their property by adding it to yours. Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, as-Suddī and Sufyān ibn Ḥassīn said it means: do not mix the two together so that you eat up both. Other explanations say the same, do not absorb it into your own property by combining them.

**"For this would indeed be a great sin"**. The Arabic word is ḥūb. Ibn ʿAbbās said that it comes from the Ethiopian language and means a major sin, and that Arabic uses it in the same sense. He called it a major and weighty sin. The same meaning was given by Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū Mālik, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Sinān. Adding their property to yours is a grave sin and a major mistake, so avoid it. Other explanations call it a great crime before Allah, and say that it will be met by Allah's punishment.

The words cover every unlawful taking or use of an orphan's property. It makes no difference whether it comes from neglecting to look after it, from swapping bad for good, or from pooling it with one's own. The stern warning for those who devour orphans' property comes later in the same passage (4:10).

### What a guardian must do

If an orphan owns property, either given to him or received through inheritance, the duty of protecting both the property and the child falls on the guardian. It makes no difference whether the father appointed the guardian before he died or the government did. The guardian must see that the child's necessary upkeep is covered. But he must not put the property into the child's hands before maturity, because an immature child may lose it somewhere.

So "give orphans their wealth" does not mean handing it over at once. A little later the surah says when: once it is certain that they have become mature and are able to tell what is good for them from what is not. The command here therefore means to protect the property, so that it can be given to them at the right time.

The verse also hints at how far a guardian's duty goes. It is not enough that he does not eat up or squander the orphan's property himself. He must do everything he can to guard it and keep it in good condition, so that it can be handed over to the orphan when he is grown.

### Swapping good for bad

Some people left the number of the orphan's possessions unchanged, but took something good out of them and put something bad of their own in its place. They would swap a lean goat for a healthy one, or a bad coin for a good one. This is also a breach of trust. A person driven by his lower self might excuse it by saying that he did not take what belonged to the orphan, he only exchanged it. The Qur'an forbids it in plain words.

The ban is wider than the swap itself. It also covers any deal the guardian makes with someone else that ends in a loss for the orphan.

A related wrong is the unfair division of shared property. It is a major sin to divide property that is held jointly so that some people receive valuable shares and others receive worthless ones, only so that the list of items adds up.

### Mixing the accounts

The words "mixing their wealth with your own" forbid eating up the orphan's property by any impermissible means. It makes no difference whether it is taken from property held jointly or from property held apart. The common practice was for the guardian to keep the orphan's property together with his own, eat from it himself and let the orphan eat from it too. There was no separate accounting, so even a practising Muslim might think there was no sin in it. That is why the prohibition on pooling is stated here.

The warning gives two choices. One is to keep the orphan's property completely separate and to spend from it separately, so that there is no danger of taking too much. The other is to run a shared household budget, but then the accounts must be so clear that one can be sure nothing belonging to the orphan was spent on oneself or for one's own benefit. A longer discussion of this appears in the passage on 2:220, in section 27 of Al-Baqarah.

The wording also hints that the people who misuse orphans' property are generally people who have property of their own. By implication they are reproached for stooping to eat up an orphan's property unlawfully when their own lawful belongings are at hand, and that is a shameful act.

### Why the verse says "eat"

The verse speaks of "eating" the orphan's property because eating is one of the main ways property is used up. In everyday speech, though, every kind of using, consuming and exhausting is called "eating up", whether it is done by eating or by any other use. The Qur'an's words "do not eat up", lā taʾkulū, carry this broad sense, and it takes in every impermissible use. Spending anything from an orphan's property unlawfully, by any means at all, is ḥarām, forbidden.

### The uncle from Ghaṭafān

Muqātil and al-Kalbī said that the verse was revealed about a man from Ghaṭafān who held a large fortune that belonged to his orphaned nephew. When the nephew reached puberty he asked for the fortune, and his uncle refused. They took their dispute to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. When the uncle heard it, he said, "We obey Allah and we obey His Messenger. We seek refuge in Allah from the great peril." Then he handed the wealth over to his nephew. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever is saved from the stinginess of his own self and does what he did will abide in Allah's Garden."

When the young man received his fortune, he spent it in the way of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said, "The reward is confirmed, but the sin still persists." Some people asked, "O Messenger of Allah, we know the reward is confirmed. How can the sin still persist when he is spending his wealth in the way of Allah?" He answered, "The reward is confirmed for the young man, while the sin persists for his father."

Another account says that when the man from Ghaṭafān heard the verse, he decided to separate his nephew's wealth from his own, for fear of committing a sin. A third says that the verse came down about an orphan who asked his guardian for his property and was refused.

After it was revealed, some guardians found it hard to keep up their guardianship of orphans. Some of them had eight or ten wives in their care and did not treat them all equally. The next verse was revealed in response.

### The inner reading

Whoever is given charge over others and then deals unjustly with those under his care will find that his opponent is his Lord. Allah takes revenge for His servants in a way He does not take revenge for His own sake. If the protector of an orphan acts with justice and kindness, Allah guards his right. If he behaves badly and with aggression, Allah is his adversary.

### In short

- Orphans, children whose fathers have died, must have their property protected and handed over in full when they come of age and show sound judgement. The guardian must not use any of it.
- Three things are forbidden: swapping one's bad possessions for the orphan's good ones, mixing the orphan's wealth with one's own so as to eat up both, and any deal that causes the orphan a loss. "Eating" stands for every unlawful use.
- A guardian should either keep the accounts completely separate or keep them so clear that no doubt remains. Doing otherwise is a great sin, and a stern warning follows later (4:10).
- The verse is said to have come down about a man from Ghaṭafān and his orphaned nephew. The uncle obeyed and handed over the fortune.
- On its inner side, Allah Himself is the opponent of a guardian who wrongs those in his charge.
